options: Any integration that moves data in real time rather than on a schedule
A direct connection between exactly two systems, with no shared intermediary layer doing translation or routing
An integration that only Salesforce can initiate, never the other system
Any integration that uses REST rather than SOAP
questions.explain: Point-to-point integration connects exactly two systems directly, with each connection built and maintained as its own self-contained piece of work and no shared middleware layer between them.

questions.q: With 6 systems that all need to exchange data with each other, roughly how many point-to-point connections would a fully-meshed design require, using N×(N-1)/2?
options: 6 connections
12 connections
15 connections
36 connections
questions.explain: N×(N-1)/2 with N=6 gives 6×5/2 = 15 connections — illustrating how quickly the connection count outgrows the system count as more systems are added.

questions.q: Besides the raw number of connections, what quieter cost does this lesson say compounds the N-squared problem?
options: Point-to-point connections always use more network bandwidth than middleware-based integrations
Each connection typically reimplements its own error handling, retry logic, authentication, and logging, so a systemic fix has to be applied to every connection individually
Point-to-point connections cannot be secured with standard authentication methods
Point-to-point connections are always slower than middleware-routed ones
questions.explain: Without a shared layer, each point-to-point connection reinvents its own error handling, retries, authentication, and logging — so improving any of those systemically means touching every connection separately instead of fixing it once.

questions.q: According to this lesson, is point-to-point integration ever still the correct architectural choice?
options: No, modern architecture practice considers point-to-point integration always a mistake

Yes, it remains correct when the number of connections is genuinely small and stable, latency is critical, the integration is unlikely to be reused by a third system, or there's a hard deadline disproportionate to adding middleware
Yes, but only for integrations that move fewer than 10 records per day
No, point-to-point integration was deprecated in favor of iPaaS tools
questions.explain: Point-to-point remains the right call for genuinely small, stable integration landscapes, latency-critical flows, one-off connections unlikely to be reused, or tight deadlines — the lesson is not that it's always wrong, only that it scales badly.

questions.q: What is the main architectural judgment call this lesson says an architect needs to make about point-to-point connections?
options: Deciding which programming language to use for each connection

Recognizing when the number of connections is about to cross from manageable into N-squared territory, so a middleware or hub-and-spoke layer can be introduced before the landscape becomes unmanageable
Deciding whether to use SOAP or REST for every new connection
Deciding how many servers to provision for each point-to-point connection
questions.explain: The judgment call is timing — recognizing the inflection point where connections are about to multiply past what's manageable, and introducing a shared middleware layer before the landscape becomes unmanageable rather than after.
